claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has a dual-phase lamellar microstructure.
Internal lamellar-colony boundaries act as microcrack nucleation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Ultrasonic-vibration-assisted rapid solidification will refine lamellar-colony boundaries.
Ultrasonic-vibration-assisted rapid solidification will induce controlled serration of lamellar-colony boundaries.
Ultrasonic vibration during rapid solidification enhances nucleation.
Ultrasonic vibration during rapid solidification enhances interfacial diffusion and bonding.
Refined, serrated internal boundaries redistribute local tensile strain and blunt stress concentrations.
Modified lamellar boundaries provide additional obstacles to dislocation motion.
The boundary modification will impede microcrack initiation and propagation.
Ultrasonic-treated material will have higher ultimate tensile strength than the conventional rapid-solidification baseline.
Ultrasonic-treated material will have greater room-temperature strain to failure than the baseline.
Ultrasonic-treated material will exhibit lower microcrack density at internal boundaries than the baseline.
Conventionally rapid-solidified eutectic high-entropy alloys exhibit increased strength but limited ductility because of microcrack initiation at unmodified lamellar-colony boundaries.
The beneficial effects will persist only while the refined, serrated microstructure remains stable against coarsening.
The proposed improvement is restricted to room-temperature tensile loading.
The magnitude of improvement depends on ultrasonic frequency, amplitude, and processing duration.
Failure to obtain statistically significant improvements in both strength and ductility relative to a conventionally processed control would falsify the hypothesis.
Increased microcracking or interfacial embrittlement after ultrasonic treatment would falsify the hypothesis.
